analysis.one_liner: Temporarily boosts the child tax credit for low-income families and restores tax breaks for business research and equipment spending.
analysis.headline: The House passed the tax deal 357-70, but the Senate never voted on it: a 48-44 procedural vote on August 1 fell 12 short of the 60 needed to move it forward, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a bipartisan tax package. For families, it increased the refundable child tax credit to $1,800-$2,000 per child and let parents use last year's income to qualify for the earned income tax credit when their income drops. For businesses, it restored immediate write-offs for research spending and let companies deduct the full cost of new equipment. It also made disaster payments tax-free for wildfire victims and residents of East Palestine, Ohio, expanded the low-income housing tax credit, and set up a tax agreement with Taiwan. It passed the House overwhelmingly but was never allowed a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income families with children, especially larger families and parents whose earnings fell; victims of wildfires and the East Palestine train derailment; businesses that spend heavily on research or new equipment; and developers building low-income housing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income families, disaster victims, and businesses

how_it_helps.text: The refundable child tax credit rises to $1,800 (2023), $1,900 (2024), and $2,000 (2025) per child, and the credit is now calculated per child rather than per return, which helps larger low-income families most.
Parents can elect to use their prior year's earned income for the child tax credit and earned income tax credit in 2024 and 2025, so a parent whose wages dropped still qualifies.
Payments for wildfire losses and payments to victims of the East Palestine train derailment (including from Norfolk Southern) are excluded from taxable income for 2020 through 2025.

The bill restores immediate expensing of domestic research costs (reversing a rule that forces five-year spreading) and extends 100% bonus depreciation through 2026, letting businesses deduct the full cost of research and new equipment right away.
The low-income housing tax credit ceiling rises to 12.5% for 2023-2025 and the bond-financing threshold drops to 30%, expanding the subsidy available for affordable rental construction.
Independent contractors get a higher reporting threshold: businesses only have to send a 1099 for payments of $1,000 or more instead of $600.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of the tax cuts, and taxpayers at large eventually carry that through deficits. Families with no earnings at all get nothing from the child credit changes, since it depends on work income. Tax preparers and firms that aggressively promoted the COVID employee retention credit face new penalties up to the greater of $200,000 or 75% of their income from the practice.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal Treasury; poor families without earnings

drawbacks.text: The family tax help is temporary and work-based: the enhanced credit only covers tax years 2023-2025 and the refundable credit requires earned income, so families with no earnings receive nothing from these changes.

The business provisions are larger in dollar terms and partly retroactive: immediate research expensing applies to costs incurred from 2022 through 2026, and bonus depreciation runs through 2026, both cutting federal revenue.

The bill authorizes the President to negotiate a tax agreement with Taiwan through a process that bypasses normal Senate treaty ratification, a departure from the more than sixty existing tax treaties, though the agreement still cannot take effect without new legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The help for working families, disaster victims, and affordable housing is real but modest and short-lived, and it excludes the poorest families who have no earnings. The business tax provisions are the bigger and longer-lasting part of the package and shrink federal revenue. As a negotiated trade, it delivered targeted help to working households while handing substantial, partly retroactive breaks to business — and in the end, none of it took effect at all.

outcome.mechanism: After passing the House 357-70, the bill sat on the Senate calendar for six months; when the Majority Leader finally forced a vote on August 1, a 48-44 procedural vote fell short of the 60 needed just to bring the bill to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Ways and Means Committee approved the bill 40-3 on January 19, 2024, and reported it four days later.
The House passed it 357-70 on January 31, 2024, under a procedure requiring a two-thirds majority: 188 Democrats and 169 Republicans voted yes.
The Senate received the bill on February 1 and placed it on its calendar, but took no action for nearly six months; the first motion to proceed came on July 29.
On August 1, 2024, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 48-44, short of the 60 votes needed; 43 of 44 voting Democrats supported it while 41 of 44 voting Republicans opposed it.
The Senate never brought the bill to a vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the revenue the tax cuts would have cost, and firms that promoted the COVID employee retention credit avoided the new penalties and the January 31, 2024 claim deadline the bill would have imposed. Working families with children came out behind: the expanded credit never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury and COVID-credit promoter firms

for.name: Jason Smith
for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, negotiated the bipartisan tax deal with the committee's ranking member, steered it through committee (40-3) and the House floor (357-70).

for.name: Richard Neal
for.role: Ranking Member, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Reached the bipartisan agreement with Chair Smith and was allotted time to control part of the House floor debate in support of the bill.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Made the motion to proceed on July 29 and filed the cloture motion to force the Senate to consider the bill, then moved to reconsider after the failed vote.

for.name: House Democratic and Republican members
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill under a rule requiring a two-thirds majority: 188 of 211 voting Democrats and 169 of 216 voting Republicans in favor.

against.name: Senate Republican caucus
against.what_they_did: Voted against cloture on the motion to proceed on August 1, 2024, denying the bill the 60 votes needed to reach the Senate floor for any vote at all.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Led Senate Republican opposition to the negotiated terms, pressing for a different balance on the business tax provisions and the child credit.

against.name: Senate opponents of the child credit terms
against.role: A bloc of Senate Republicans and a few Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Objected to the child tax credit terms — including how it treats children without Social Security numbers — and to the relative size of the business provisions, preventing agreement on floor procedure.

sides.party_line_note: In the House the bill was genuinely bipartisan, passing 357-70 with 188 Democrats and 169 Republicans in favor; in the Senate the fight split by party, with Democrats voting 43-1 to proceed and Republicans voting 41-3 to block.

industries.note: The bill restores immediate deduction of domestic research costs, reversing the five-year spreading rule that took effect in 2022, retroactively for 2022-2026. The gain comes partly at the cost of federal revenue, though supporters argued it protected U.S. research jobs.
100% bonus depreciation is extended through 2026 and small-business expensing limits rise, letting companies deduct equipment costs immediately rather than over years.

industries.industry: Low-income housing developers and tax credit investors
industries.note: The bill enlarges the low-income housing tax credit and eases the bond-financing threshold, increasing the subsidy that flows through private developers to build affordable rentals. It keeps the system's reliance on private investors intact while expanding it.

industries.industry: Wildfire victims and East Palestine residents
industries.note: Compensation for wildfire losses and payments from Norfolk Southern for the 2023 derailment would be tax-free, putting more of the money in victims' hands.

industries.industry: Taiwan-based companies investing in the United States
industries.note: Withholding taxes on Taiwanese investors' U.S. dividends, interest, and royalties drop from 30% to 10% (15% for many dividends), reducing double taxation and easing investment frictions.

industries.industry: COVID employee retention credit promoter firms
industries.note: The bill imposes penalties up to the greater of $200,000 or 75% of promoter income for aiding fraudulent claims, adds due-diligence requirements, and cuts off new claims after January 31, 2024.
The 1099 reporting threshold rises from $600 to $1,000 with inflation indexing, reducing paperwork for small payers, though it slightly weakens income reporting that helps catch unreported earnings.
